articles.title: ‘The only way is up’: cycling Norway’s mountainous ‘Milky Way’
articles.summary: The Mjølkevegen was once used to bring milk from high pastures to the towns below. Now cyclists are discovering the road’s breathtaking panoramas of peaks and lakes, dotted with cosy inns. ‘Norway is a hilly country,” shrugs Glenn Roar Berge. He’s not wrong, though he is fond of an understatement.
body: For most of our three-day ride, we’ll be following the Mjølkevegen, or Milky Way, a 155-mile (250km) route from Vinstra in the north to Gol in the south. It was developed after the second world war, when increased demand for fresh milk meant connecting the mountain farms with the towns below. While farming continues, the road has been embraced in recent years by gravel cyclists, (typically riders on drop-bar bikes favouring unpaved roads and trails), looking for a multi-day adventure far from towns and cities.

Ruten Fjellstue is a traditional inn, set up for cross-country skiing in winter, hiking and biking in summer. My trip starts here and it’s where I’ll meet my guide and group, and pick up my hired bike. It’s set high above the valley and painted falun red – the iron-oxide agricultural paint typical across Nordic countries. Berit and Arthur are the third-generation owners. I arrive late, so Arthur picks me up from Vinstra train station (about three hours north-west of Oslo) and Berit has kept a home-cooked meal warm: a generous plate of fish with potatoes, vegetables and cream sauce, followed by apple crumble.

articles.title: Monstera magic: Barbican hands out cuttings as ‘green lung of the city’ closes
articles.summary: Five hundred people turn up to adopt plants from conservatory that will reopen in 2030 after renovation project. Above the waxy monstera leaves and bright pink hibiscus flowers in the Barbican conservatory hangs a giant net to catch the panes of glass that are at risk of falling from the ceiling on…
body: This precarious situation has caused the estate to shutter its greenhouse on the third and fourth floors for three years so a full refurbishment can take place. But the hiatus has a silver lining for many of those who visited on Wednesday to give the plants from the conservatory a new home.
Five hundred people turned up to pick up a cutting from the Barbican’s plant collection and were asked to fill out an “adoption form” as if they were taking home a pet.
Lydia Goldberg, 56, a tech worker, was one of the first through the door and selected a pretty, silvery-green Swedish ivy plant.

“I am a houseplant lover,” she said. “I live in the Barbican and my bedroom overlooks the conservatory. I am sad to see it close but it’s great that it’s being restored. Having a piece of the conservatory in my flat will be incredible and this is a real community event. I can see quite a few of my neighbours here!”

articles.title: It used to be our imperfect bodies that made us insecure. With AI, it’s our minds as well
articles.summary: For most of modern history, technology sought to imitate humans. Humans increasingly seek to imitate technology. Two faces that appeared on my Instagram feed in recent months gave me pause. One belonged to John Travolta at Cannes.
body: In any case the feeling lasted only a second: a flicker of unease, as though I were looking at people who had become approximations of themselves.

There is a name for that sensation. In a 1970 article, the Japanese robotics professor Masahiro Mori described what he called the “uncanny valley”. He found that robots that were designed to look as human as possible often provoked discomfort in people. That was a surprise, since the benefit of humanoid robots was supposed to be that we humans would trust them more.

What scares us about a robot that almost passes as human? One explanation may be that we sense danger when encountering something we cannot categorise easily as either human or not. Another is that the features that seem “off”, such as glossy skin or frozen expressions, resemble signs of disease or death.
points: For most of modern history, technology sought to imitate humans.

articles.title: You be the judge: should my partner stop hogging my side of the bed?
articles.summary: Pádraig has a favourite side, whereas Dave likes to sleep farthest from the door. Help us put this argument to bed • Find out how to get a disagreement settled or become a juror. I sleep better on the left side of the bed. I shouldn’t have to swap just because we’ve moved to a new flat.
body: My partner Dave and I are two stubborn boys who both adore a great night’s sleep. But we cannot settle a disagreement about which side of the bed belongs to whom. We’ve recently moved into a new flat and the orientation of our room and bed has shifted. Now, the side of the bed I assumed was mine has become Dave’s.

We lived in our old flat for three and a half years. We slept like kings there: a humongous bed and individual duvets, which our Swedish friend had recommended for a good night’s sleep. I was on the left side (if you were standing at the foot of the bed facing it). I felt well rested and got into a great sleep routine.

Due to the orientation of our new bedroom, Dave wants to be furthest from the door, so I’m now sleeping on the right side and he is on the left. He thinks the sides we sleep on should be interchangeable, depending on where the door is, but I say the left side is mine, no matter what. So I’ve been forced to sleep on what I deem to be the wrong side for the last few months. I find it challenging to fall asleep and can’t get used to it.
points: Pádraig has a favourite side, whereas Dave likes to sleep farthest from the door.

articles.title: It’s Time for Brands to Invest in Women Who Lift
articles.summary: As GLP-1 users look to build muscle mass, and strength training appears more readily in popular culture, it could be time for luxury brands to hit the gym.
body: When French fashion house Mugler launched its first-ever handbag in June, it did so with a bold campaign. In it, Tatiana Horslaville, a female bodybuilder, was photographed naked — the lighting casting exquisite shadows across her sculpted physique, which rippled with muscle, tissue and veins. Her arms flexed as she carried the black, rectangular Aurora bag, imitating an outer dumbbell curl. It was disarming and disruptive, especially for an industry where size inclusivity is clearly treated as a passing trend.

For Adrian Corsin, Mugler’s managing director, the rarity of this physique in women’s fashion brought something “fresh” in a sea of sameness. “A muscular femininity feels new in a world dominated with important discourse about body positivity, peptides, and overall health,” he says. The main character of the campaign was not the bag, but the body.
points: As GLP-1 users look to build muscle mass, and strength training appears more readily in popular culture, it could be time for luxury brands to hit the gym.

articles.title: Should Luxury Brands Reduce their Prices?
articles.summary: Luxury price hikes alienated the aspirational shopper. After Gucci lowered the price on its Mercato bag, it begs the question, should other brands follow suit?
body: Earlier this year, a medium leather Gucci Mercato tote bag, designed by Demna for Spring/Summer 2026, would have set you back $2,900. But in May, analysts at Bernstein noticed a shift: Gucci had quietly reduced the price of the tote by an estimated 20-25%.

The move was part of a wider turnaround strategy for Gucci and parent company Kering to boost sales volume and re-address the aspirational shopper, as outlined at the group’s Capital Markets Day in April. As the broader luxury market aims to re-address the 50 million luxury shoppers lost amid post-pandemic price hikes, is reducing prices the way to course correct?

During the pandemic boom era, most luxury labels sought to boost margins with price hikes across their goods. According to HSBC, the average price of personal luxury goods increased by a staggering 52% between 2019 and 2024.
points: After Gucci lowered the price on its Mercato bag, it begs the question, should other brands follow suit?

articles.title: On Her New Album ‘Blue Island,’ Ravyn Lenae Proves She Can Do It All
articles.summary: The genre-defying musician is back with a standout third record that serves a riposte to those who have previously tried to pigeonhole her as a Black artist.
body: For a long time, Lenae may indeed have felt she was more than mainstream audiences could handle. Hailing from the Chicago suburbs, she’s been releasing music for over a decade, beginning with underground R&B EPs and eventually leading to her first full-length album, 2022’s Steve Lacy and Kaytranada-assisted Hypnos, which landed on multiple year-end best-of lists, but didn’t quite get the traction she’d hoped for. Then came her 2024 follow-up, Bird’s Eye, which kicked off with the global smash hit (and TikTok-viral) single “Love Me Not,” and led to a stint supporting Sabrina Carpenter and a stratospheric rise to fame for Lenae.

Instead of riding that wave to work with blue-chip pop producers, however, Lenae saw it as an opportunity to take stock. Heading back to her hometown of Blue Island, Illinois (hence the album’s title), she regrouped with her longtime collaborator Dahi to make a record that reflects her personal growth during that whirlwind time, from coming to terms with the end of a long-term relationship to adjusting to the sudden rise of voices online telling her what she should do next and who she should be as an artist.
points: The genre-defying musician is back with a standout third record that serves a riposte to those who have previously tried to pigeonhole her as a Black artist.

articles.title: Why Anthony Bourdain’s Editor Wanted ‘Tony’ to Be Darker
articles.summary: There are two types of biopics: those that unconventionally show, and those that exhaustively tell. Thank goodness that Tony, the highly anticipated A24 biopic about the late Anthony Bourdain, takes the former route.
body: Eater spoke with the film’s screenwriters about casting the titular role, chef cameos, and more BTS moments.

Then again, successfully pitching a Bourdain biopic to his estate was always going to be a big swing. I spoke with Todd Bartels and Lou Howe about what made that swing possible (for one: bringing on Kimberly Witherspoon, Bourdain’s literary agent and friend, as an executive producer); which cast member demonstrated the best culinary chops; and who they could imagine playing an older, more seasoned Anthony Bourdain.
Eater: How did you strike the balance between making a movie for the passionate Anthony Bourdain fans, and viewers who may know very little about him?

Lou Howe: I was anxious about that [ laughs ], especially at the very beginning. But [we] just [tried] to make a good movie, and hope that the entertainment factor and emotional engagement hits the target well enough. We started this whole process as fans, so in that way we felt relatively comfortable servicing fellow fans. You want to write a good story that people can plug into no matter who the character is. Of course, there are some Kitchen Confidential Easter eggs.
points: There are two types of biopics: those that unconventionally show, and those that exhaustively tell.
Thank goodness that Tony, the highly anticipated A24 biopic about the late Anthony Bourdain, takes the former route.

articles.title: 5 Exciting Hotel Openings on the Mediterranean Coast That Are a Design Lover's Dream
articles.summary: The most exciting hotels opening in Southern Europe put local heritage and artisanship first.
body: Opened in May, this escape is the brainchild of Christopher and Suzanne Sharp, the founders of The Rug Company. She was born on the island, they bought the 18th-century palazzo together in 2010, and he spent the years since filling the gardens with jasmine and bougainvillea. In the way that Malta has long lived at the crossroads of Europe, so too does the characterful 17-room property. Hand-painted pottery from nearby ceramics studio Villa Bologna (owned by Sharp scion Sophie) share rooms with Sicilian marble tables and glass fixtures from Murano.

This May, Zannier added to its smattering of immersive design hotels a 17-acre private island along the Côte d'Azur. Owned by the Ricard family of Pastis fame, it's now a beautiful, laid-back retreat steeped in Provençal tradition. A ferry connects the mainland to this car-free village-as-resort, where existing structures like two-story former fishermen's houses are now villas courtesy of Paris firms Hardel Le Bihan Architectes and Niez Studio Paysagistes. Crafts workshops for guests are held three times a week in a converted warehouse.

articles.title: 7 All-Inclusive Resorts in the US That Are Worth the Splurge
articles.summary: From a Montana cattle ranch to a Sedona canyon retreat, these American resorts prove the US can do all-in-one vacations just as well as the tropics.
body: I love piecing a trip together myself, mapping out every restaurant reservation and day trip until the itinerary is exactly right. But over the years—and especially since becoming a mom —I've come to appreciate what an all-inclusive resort takes off my plate. These properties fold your room, meals, drinks, and often your activities into one upfront rate, so you're not doing math over a glass of wine or budgeting out an afternoon of kayaking. You know your total cost before you land, and you get to actually be present with your family instead of managing a running tab and a packed schedule.
Included in the rate: Three farm-to-table meals daily, afternoon tea, guided hikes, an indoor pool, boating, golf, and most outdoor activities; alcohol and spa treatments cost extra.

Why we love it: This Victorian-era castle sits on its own lake and comes with 85 miles of hiking trails and a nine-hole golf course—all folded into the nightly rate. It's also one of the more accessible drives on this list, about 90 miles from New York City, so it's an easy sell for a long weekend without a flight.
points: From a Montana cattle ranch to a Sedona canyon retreat, these American resorts prove the US can do all-in-one vacations just as well as the tropics.
